meta.location: The road to Manti; the wilderness; the land of Ishmael; the waters of Sebus
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)

world_behind.title: The chapter is a hinge and a flashback
world_behind.text: Alma meets the sons of Mosiah on a road in verse 1, and by verse 6 the record has jumped back fourteen years to their departure. Everything from here to Alma 26 is that missing stretch, told out of sequence and folded into Alma's own story.

world_behind.title: They turned down a kingdom
world_behind.text: Verse 6 notes that they refused the throne their father offered and the people wanted them to take. That refusal is what ended the monarchy and produced the system of judges the book has been running on for sixteen chapters.

world_behind.title: They armed themselves for food, and the record says so
world_behind.text: Verse 7 lists swords, spears, bows, arrows and slings, then explains the purpose: provisions in the wilderness. The clarification matters given what Ammon does with a sling and a sword twenty-nine verses later.

world_behind.title: Fourteen years is stated before any of it is shown
world_behind.text: Verse 4 gives the duration and the result up front. The reader knows the mission succeeded before learning that Ammon spent his first three days as a herdsman.

world_behind.title: The Lamanite portrait is unflattering and then qualified
world_behind.text: Verses 14 and 15 call them wild, hardened, ferocious and indolent, and then verse 15 supplies the cause in what their fathers handed down, with the Lord's promises still open on conditions of repentance. Alma 9 made the same two moves in the same order.

world_behind.title: Binding captives was routine
world_behind.text: Verse 20 says taking Nephites and carrying them before the king was the Lamanite custom, and that killing or enslaving them was the king's choice. Ammon walks into a known procedure.

world_behind.title: The water was contested and people had died over it
world_behind.text: Verse 26 says all the Lamanites drove their flocks to Sebus, and verse 28 has servants weeping because the king has killed men before for losing flocks there. The scattering is an established racket with a known body count.

words.text: A tool in another hand. The sons of Mosiah ask for the Spirit in some measure, enough to make them "an instrument in the hands of God" (v. 9), and the Lord uses the same word back to them two verses later. The image gives up agency about the outcome while keeping all of it about the willingness. That is the posture the next ten chapters require.

cites.quote: an instrument in the hands of God

spans.text: an instrument in the hands of God

words.text: Lowness of condition and of character. The word appears once in this record and never in the King James Bible. It sits inside the prayer of the sons of Mosiah: a portion of the Spirit, so they might go among the Lamanites and correct their baseness. They use the word while asking for help rather than while describing an enemy.

Savage, given to violence. The word is absent from the King James Bible and this record uses it six times, always of the Lamanites or of people who have gone that way. It arrives here inside a list the chapter will spend ten chapters dismantling, and the record puts it in the mouths of no one. It is the narrator's own word.

Idle, disinclined to work. It occurs once in all of scripture, here. The charge is economic before it is moral, and the verse pairs it with idol worship and the traditions of the fathers. The record is describing a way of life, and that is why it can also say the promises were still open.

Assigned posts. Ammon "blessed them according to their several stations" (v. 18) before they scattered, and the noun occurs nowhere else in scripture. It implies an assignment made in advance: each man had a place, and the blessing was fitted to it.

cites.quote: blessed them according to their several stations

spans.text: blessed them according to their several stations

words.text: In older use, to soothe or encourage, without the modern taint. Ammon "flattered them by his words" (v. 31), and the verse then quotes the words: be of good cheer, let us go find the flocks. What follows is a rescue. The King James Bible uses the family of words for deceit, and the older sense here is easy to misread because of it.

phrases.term: They had waxed strong in the knowledge of the truth
phrases.text: Alma's joy has two parts and the second is the surprise: they were still his brethren in the Lord. Fourteen years apart, and what he finds is growth. The verse credits searching the scriptures diligently for it.

Listed alongside hunger, thirst and fatigue as one of the afflictions. The record puts inward work in the same sentence as physical deprivation and does not rank them. It is the only item on the list nobody could have seen.

phrases.term: Be comforted. And they were comforted
phrases.text: The shortest exchange in the chapter and possibly in the book. God says two words; the record reports the result in four. Nothing is explained about how, and the sentence structure refuses to make it complicated.

phrases.term: Show forth good examples unto them in me
phrases.text: The instruction that shapes the whole mission. Patience in long-suffering and afflictions comes first, and the promise of being made an instrument comes after. The order says the example is the method.

phrases.term: Meet again at the close of their harvest
phrases.text: Farming language for a fourteen-year separation. They part at the border trusting they will see each other when the work is done. Christ uses the same figure of fields white already to harvest. Alma 26 records the reunion the verse anticipates.

phrases.term: Nay, but I will be thy servant
phrases.text: Ammon's answer to the offer of a royal marriage. He turns down entry into the family and asks for the bottom of the household instead. The whole strategy of the next three chapters is decided in six words.

phrases.term: His heart was swollen within him with joy
phrases.text: Reported at the moment the servants are weeping and expecting to die. The record explains the reaction in the next clause: he sees a chance to show the power in him. Verse 30 then says he called these men his brethren, the only warrant the text gives for the joy.

phrases.term: Bearing the arms which had been smitten off
phrases.text: The chapter ends on an image it does not soften. The servants carry severed arms to the king as testimony. What convinces a court, in this account, is physical evidence brought in by witnesses who were there.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: The method is dispersal, and the authority is individual
verses.text: "They separated themselves one from another, and went forth among them, every man alone." A company that had travelled together for years splits to work singly, and the warrant is issued per person, "according to the word and power of God which was given unto him." The record does not describe a mission. It describes several.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: A title is withdrawn and a function put in its place
verses.text: "Ammon being the chief among them, or rather he did administer unto them." The sentence corrects itself in front of the reader, and what it trades away is rank. This volume makes that repair twelve times; Mosiah 7:8 uses it to turn a permission into an order, and here it turns a chief into a servant, eight verses before Ammon says the word himself.

verses.label: v. 26–27
verses.title: Three days of service, then the water
verses.text: The record counts the interval before the incident, and describes the place as shared infrastructure: all the Lamanites drive their flocks there. The scattering that follows is not an accident of geography but a use of it, and the verse explains the arrangement before anyone exploits it.

verses.label: v. 28–29
verses.title: Two reactions to one event, and a stated strategy
verses.text: The servants weep, and the record gives their reasoning: the king has killed men for this before. Ammon's heart "was swollen within him with joy," and the record gives his reasoning too, in his own words, that restoring the flocks will win their hearts "that I may lead them to believe in my words." The motive is printed as calculation, and nothing in the chapter apologises for it.

chapter.title: The mission is stated backwards
chapter.text: Success is announced in verse 4 and the story starts in verse 6. The record removes suspense on purpose, which frees the reader to watch how it was done.

chapter.title: Preparation is the chapter's real subject
chapter.text: Prayer, fasting, searching the scriptures, fourteen years of it, all reported before a single Lamanite is met. The famous scene at the water is four verses. The preparation is five times longer.

chapter.title: The refusal of the kingdom holds up the whole book
chapter.text: Verse 6 dates the departure and states the refusal in the same clause, "having taken leave of their father, Mosiah, in the first year of the judges; having refused the kingdom which their father was desirous to confer upon them." That refusal is what Mosiah 29 spends forty-seven verses converting into a system of judges, and Alma 1 through 16 is the history of that system. The mission narrative and the constitutional history begin in the same sentence.

chapter.title: Ammon asks for the lowest position available
chapter.text: The king offers "one of his daughters to wife" at verse 24 and the answer at verse 25 is four words, "Nay, but I will be thy servant." The record then records the posting, "he was set among other servants to watch the flocks." Everything at the waters of Sebus and in the king's house follows from that assignment, so the access is obtained by declining the higher offer.

chapter.title: The portrait is harsh and the verdict is open
chapter.text: Verses 14 and 15 pile up the charges, "a wild and a hardened and a ferocious people," "a very indolent people, many of whom did worship idols," and then verse 15 ends with a clause that reverses the direction, "notwithstanding the promises of the Lord were extended unto them on the conditions of repentance." The same pairing stands at Alma 9:16, where the traditions of their fathers are named as the cause. A low estimate and an open door are held in one sentence.

chapter.title: The joy at the water is explained, and the explanation is fraternal
chapter.text: Ammon is glad because he can show his power, and verse 30 says he had already begun calling these servants his brethren. The record supplies the motive.

chapter.title: The chapter ends with evidence
chapter.text: No preaching has happened yet. What reaches the king is a pile of severed arms and the testimony of men who watched. The teaching begins in the next chapter, on ground the fighting bought.

applications.title: Count the preparation
applications.text: Fourteen years is the interval, and the record names what filled it, "much prayer, and fasting," with the result stated as a consequence, "therefore they had the spirit of prophecy." Whatever you want to be able to do, the chapter's assumption is that the capacity was built beforehand.

applications.title: Ask for a portion rather than for the outcome
applications.text: What they prayed for on the road was "a portion of his Spirit to go with them," not success. The answer at verse 10 is two words, "Be comforted," and the record adds that they were.

applications.title: Take the instruction that comes with the assignment
applications.text: The errand is given with a manner attached, "ye shall be patient in long-suffering and afflictions, that ye may show forth good examples." The how is part of the what, and it is stated before anything happens.

applications.title: Separate and trust the meeting
applications.text: They split up at the border, "trusting in the Lord that they should meet again." Work that has to be done in several places at once requires being willing to lose sight of the others.

applications.title: Ask for the lower position
applications.text: Offered a daughter of the king, Ammon answers in four words, "Nay, but I will be thy servant," and is posted to the flocks. Every later thing he accomplishes runs through an access obtained by asking for less.

applications.title: Let someone's fear be your reason
applications.text: What made Ammon glad was other men weeping, "for, said he, I will show forth my power unto these my fellow-servants." The opportunity he saw was somebody else's emergency, and he named it as such.

applications.title: Encourage before you organize
applications.text: Ammon's first move with frightened men is a sentence, "My brethren, be of good cheer," and only then the plan to gather the flocks. People will not execute a plan they are too afraid to hear.

applications.title: Do the ordinary next job
applications.text: After the fight he waters the flocks, returns them to pasture, and goes in to the king carrying the arms. The remarkable thing is finished by the unremarkable one, and the record reports both in the same verse.

questions.text: Who would be surprised, if they met me after fourteen years, by where I have ended up spiritually, and in which direction?
What labor of mine has been in the spirit and invisible, and do I count it as real work?
What have I been offered that I would need to refuse in order to do the thing I actually believe in?
When was I last comforted quickly and simply, and did I let it be that simple?
Whom am I trusting to meet again at the close of the harvest, and have I told them so?
What position am I holding out for that is smaller than I think it is?
Whose fear near me is an assignment I have been treating as an inconvenience?
